opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of them as deeply complementary. Generative AI, the large language models, is fundamentally about predicting what's plausible. It's extraordinarily good at that: drafting code, summarizing documents, translating between natural language and more formal representations. But plausible isn't the same as correct. These models can hallucinate, and they don't give you a guarantee about why an answer is right.

Automated reasoning comes from the other side. It's the branch of AI rooted in mathematical logic. We build tools like theorem provers, SAT and SMT solvers, and model checkers that search for proofs. When they say something is true, you get a proof you can check, and that holds over all possible inputs, not just the cases you happened to test. That's been the backbone of how we verify things like cryptography, access control policies, hypervisors, and storage systems at scale.

So the relationship I see is a kind of division of labor. Generative AI is great at the fuzzy, creative, front-end work. It can take a policy written in English and propose a formal specification, or suggest a loop invariant, or sketch a proof. Automated reasoning then acts as the checker, saying "yes, this is provably correct" or "no, here's a counterexample." That feedback can go back to the model so it tries again. You get the flexibility of neural methods and the soundness of symbolic methods together.

Some people call this neurosymbolic AI. Practically, it means we can start making generative AI trustworthy in domains where mistakes are costly, like security, compliance, finance, and healthcare. Instead of hoping the model got it right, you can prove it did, or at least know exactly where it didn't. And it goes the other way too. LLMs are lowering the barrier to using formal methods, which have historically needed a lot of specialized expertise. That's what excites me most: the two fields are making each other far more useful than either was alone.

r003.rationale: It says the fields make each other more useful, but does not identify generative AI as bringing previously separated research communities back together.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a great question, and I think it's one that's really come into focus for a lot of people over the last couple of years. The way I think about it is that these are two very different, almost complementary traditions in AI, and they've got very different strengths.

Automated reasoning comes out of the logic tradition. It goes back to Aristotle, really, and then through Boole, Frege, Gödel, Turing, and then the work in the sixties and seventies on theorem proving and SAT solving and model checking. The idea is you write down a mathematical statement, and then you have a tool that will search for a proof that the statement is true, or a counterexample showing it's false. And the key property is soundness. If the tool says something is true, it's true. You get a proof that you can check independently. It's not a probabilistic claim.

Generative AI, and large language models in particular, come out of the statistical learning tradition. They're extraordinarily good at things that automated reasoning has always been terrible at: dealing with ambiguity, natural language, intuition, generating candidates, pattern matching over enormous amounts of data. But fundamentally they're predicting likely next tokens. They're not reasoning in the formal sense, even when the output looks like reasoning. And that's where you get hallucinations. The model will confidently tell you something that's just not so.

So the way I see the relationship is that each one covers the other's weakness. The LLM is great at the creative, informal, "what should we even try" part of the problem, and the automated reasoning tool is great at the "is this actually correct" part. For decades the bottleneck in formal methods was that you needed a human expert to write the specifications, to write the invariants, to translate the fuzzy real-world thing into logic. That's expensive and slow. And it turns out LLMs are pretty good at generating those artifacts. They're not reliable at it, but they don't have to be, because you hand what they produce to a solver and the solver tells you whether it's right. If it's wrong, you loop back and try again.

Going the other direction, you can use automated reasoning to check the output of generative models. So if a model makes a claim about, say, a policy or a piece of code or a regulation, you can translate that into logic and actually prove whether it follows from the rules. That's the idea behind what we've been doing with Automated Reasoning checks at AWS. You take the thing that's inherently fuzzy and put a sound, mathematical check around it.

So I don't see it as a competition between neural and symbolic. I think the interesting work right now is at the seam between them, where the generative model proposes and the reasoning engine verifies. And I think that combination is going to be one of the things that lets us actually trust these systems in settings where being wrong really matters.

r001.rationale: The response describes the approaches as complementary and says their seam is promising, but does not predict that their conceptual boundaries will become less distinct.

r003.rationale: It describes combining generative models with reasoning engines, but does not say generative AI is bringing previously separated research communities back together.

r004.rationale: It discusses combining neural and symbolic approaches, but does not frame that integration as a return to AI’s original vision.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. Generative AI is very good at proposing things—a piece of code, an explanation, a possible solution. Automated reasoning gives us a way to ask, “Does that actually satisfy the properties we care about?” And, under explicitly stated assumptions, we can answer that with a mathematical guarantee.

For example, a model might generate a change to a program. We can then use automated reasoning to check whether that change preserves a particular security property. If it doesn’t, the reasoning tool may produce a counterexample that we can feed back to the model to help it revise the proposal.

The important qualification is that we’re proving a specific property of a particular model of the system. We still have to get those specifications and assumptions right. But combining the ability to generate candidates with the ability to check them is a very powerful direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Generative AI is remarkably good at proposing things—a piece of code, an explanation, a candidate solution. Automated reasoning gives us a way to ask, “Does this actually satisfy the properties we care about?” And, under clearly stated assumptions, we can answer that question with a mathematical proof.

Take code generation. A model can produce code that looks entirely plausible, but looking plausible isn’t the same as being correct. We can use automated reasoning to check specific properties of that code. If a property doesn’t hold, the reasoning tool can often produce a counterexample, which gives the model concrete feedback to try again.

There’s an opportunity in the other direction, too. Building a proof involves search, and models can help suggest useful steps or candidate invariants. The crucial distinction is that suggesting a proof and checking a proof are different jobs. We can let the model be creative while requiring a rigorous checker to validate the result.

So I see a very productive relationship: generative AI helps us construct candidates, and automated reasoning helps us establish precisely what we can trust about them.
